name: Laurence Brown Douglas
story: Laurence Brown Douglas is the man at the center of this book. He was born at nine o'clock on the evening of June 14, 1907, at the Royal Maternity Hospital in Lauriston Place, Edinburgh. Twenty days later his mother, Agnes Brown, registered him as Lawrence Brown. For her home she gave Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar.

By the spring of 1911 he was living at 16 Lochrin Place in Edinburgh as Laurence B. Douglas, the son of the house of Robert and Elizabeth Douglas. In 1912 the family moved to Dunfermline. He grew up there with the Douglases' daughter, Janet. Robert Douglas died of tuberculosis in 1919, and in October 1920, at thirteen, Laurence left school with an exemption and went to work as a message boy for a grocer.

In September 1929 he sailed from Greenock with Janet on the Duchess of Bedford and crossed into the United States at Detroit as Lawrence Brown, twenty-two, grocer, six feet tall, fair hair, blue eyes, fifty dollars. In Chicago he lived with Janet and her husband. By 1937 he was in Providence as a display man, dressing store windows on Weybosset Street, the trade he would follow for the rest of his life.

In October 1939 he married Constance Eugenie Darcy in Birmingham, Alabama. They lived in San Francisco, where he dressed the windows of Bond Stores, and in 1943, in a federal court in Pittsburgh, he became an American citizen as Laurence Brown Douglas: both names at once. After the war the family settled in Pawtucket and then Providence, at 644 River Avenue. He died at St. Joseph's Hospital in Providence on March 9, 1961, at fifty-three, and was buried at Saint Ann Cemetery in Cranston. His grandson, Doug Garceau, wrote this book.

name: Agnes McGarth Brown
story: Agnes McGarth Brown was Laurence's mother. She was born at half past two in the afternoon on December 18, 1885, in a ploughman's cottage at Edston, near Peebles, the second daughter of George Brown and Christina Henderson. Her father gave her his own mother's name, Agnes McGarth. He died when she was three and a half months old, and her mother took the two girls home to Libberton parish, to the row of cottages at Quothquan.

Her mother died in February 1891, when Agnes was five, and her grandmother, Jane Henderson, took her in. That June her grandmother died too. Agnes grew up in the cottage later called Lime Tree, with her sister Mary, her uncle Andrew Henderson and James Parker, the boy her grandmother had raised. A few doors along lived Mary Archibald, whose brother Alexander would become the gardener at Shieldhill House.

By 1907 Agnes was a domestic servant. On July 4, 1907, she registered her son, Lawrence Brown, in Edinburgh and gave her home as Gean Cottage, Shieldhill. In the 1901 census a similar cottage address was associated with Mary Archibald. Their household arrangements in 1906–07 remain unknown.

By 1911 she was a nurse at the Royal Edinburgh Asylum in Morningside. On August 28, 1911, she married an asylum attendant, Thomas McKay McKenzie, by declaration at Chambers Street, before the same registrar who had recorded her son's birth. They had two daughters, Mary Christina in 1912 and Jean Henderson in 1914. One portrait of her is known. Where and when she died has not yet been found.

name: George Brown
story: George Brown was Laurence's grandfather, the father of Agnes. He was born on July 18, 1862 (a date from other researchers’ family trees), one of at least ten children of William Brown, a ploughman, and Agnes McGarth, and he became a ploughman like his father. In 1871 the census found him at eight in the same household as his elder brother Lawrence Tweedie Brown.

On Friday, June 1, 1883, at twenty, he married Christina Henderson at Quothquan, in the parish of Libberton. Their first daughter, Mary Henderson Brown, was born that August. By the winter of 1885 George had found work at Edston, a farm in the parish of Lyne near Peebles, and there his second daughter, Agnes McGarth Brown, was born on December 18, 1885. He registered her himself on the last day of the year and signed as her father.

George Brown died at Edston at half past one in the morning on April 5, 1886, aged twenty-three, when Agnes was three and a half months old. His death register is the document that names his own parents. His widow took their two girls home to Libberton.

name: Christina Henderson Brown
story: Christina Henderson was Laurence's grandmother, the mother of Agnes. She was born on March 19, 1860, at Libberton, the eldest child of Alexander Henderson and Jane Robb, and grew up in the farm country under Quothquan Law, four miles from Biggar.

She married George Brown, a ploughman, at Quothquan on June 1, 1883. Eleven weeks later she gave birth to their first daughter, Mary, and went to the registrar herself. Her second daughter, Agnes, was born at Edston near Peebles in December 1885. Four months later George died, and Christina, a widow at twenty-six, took the two girls home to Libberton.
Christina died at Quothquan on February 10, 1891 (the date cut on the Henderson family stone), at thirty, eight weeks before the census found her daughters in their grandmother's cottage.

name: William Brown
story: William Brown was Laurence's great-grandfather on his mother's side. He was a ploughman in the sheep country of Peeblesshire, born about 1835, who walked behind a pair of horses turning the ground for oats and turnips and moved from farm to farm as the term days dictated. Like most farm laborers of his time, he owned no land and no house; the cottage came with the job.

He married Agnes McGarth of Tweedsmuir. They had at least ten children: William, about 1859; Lawrence Tweedie, 1860; George, 1862; then Alexander, Jane, John, James Tweedie, Agnes, Thomas and Tweedie McGarth Brown. The McGarth and Tweedie names were passed down as middle names for three generations.
Two of his sons matter to this story. George was the father of Agnes McGarth Brown, Laurence's mother. Lawrence Tweedie Brown was the uncle whose first name Agnes gave her son.

name: Agnes McGarth
story: Agnes McGarth was Laurence's great-grandmother, the wife of William Brown. She was born about 1840 at Tweedsmuir, where the Tweed rises in the hills of Peeblesshire. In 1851 the census found her in her parents' crowded house: her father, Tweedie McGarth; her mother, Jane, a woman from Wamphray in Dumfriesshire; and her brothers and sisters Jane, James Tweedie, Sarah, Ann and Janet.

She married William Brown, a ploughman, and raised at least ten children. Her son George named his second daughter for her, Agnes McGarth Brown, and so her name came down to Laurence's mother. More than a century later an indexer misread it as McGrath, but the handwriting in the register says McGarth.

name: Lawrence Tweedie Brown
story: Lawrence Tweedie Brown was the elder brother of George Brown and the uncle of Agnes McGarth Brown. He was born on September 14, 1860, at Peebles, a son of William Brown and Agnes McGarth. In 1871 the census found him at ten in the same household as his brother George.
He married Isabella Graham of Cambusnethan, raised a family at Traquair and Sanquhar, and eventually settled in Quebec, where he died in 1943.
His place in this story is his name. When Agnes registered her son in 1907, she gave him the first name Lawrence, the name of her father's elder brother.

He and Isabella had at least eight children, among them Isabella Crawford Brown (1883–1953), Agnes McGarth Brown (1886–1979), Janet Graham Brown (1888–1983), William, Elizabeth, Lawrence Tweedie and Hugh Graham Brown. Their daughter Agnes, a year younger than Laurence's mother, carried the same name, Agnes McGarth Brown, after the grandmother both girls shared. The two Agneses were first cousins and are different women.

name: Mary Henderson Brown
story: Mary Henderson Brown was Agnes's elder sister, and Laurence's aunt. She was born at Quothquan at twenty past eight on the morning of August 18, 1883, and her mother registered her herself.

Her father died when she was two and a half, and her mother when she was seven. In April 1891 the census found her, seven, and Agnes, five, in their grandmother Jane Henderson's cottage in the Castle row. In 1901, at seventeen, she was still at Lime Tree Cottage with Agnes, their uncle Andrew Henderson and James Parker. She was the one member of her own family who grew up beside Agnes from the start.

name: Jane Henderson
story: Jane Henderson, born Jane Robb, was Agnes's grandmother, and Laurence's great-grandmother. She was a crofter born at Carnwath, the wife of Alexander Henderson, and she raised her family at Libberton: Christina, Jane, Janet, David and, about 1876, a late son, Andrew.

Hers was a house that took children in. In 1881 she was raising a boy of eight, James Parker, as her own. In February 1891 her daughter Christina died, and Jane took in Christina's two girls, Mary and Agnes Brown. On census night that April she was fifty-six, in the row called Castle, with her daughter Jane, her son Andrew, James Parker and her two granddaughters.
She died on June 8, 1891, four months after her daughter. Her cottage, later called Lime Tree, remained Agnes's home until Agnes moved a few doors along to Gean Cottage.

name: Andrew Henderson
story: Andrew Henderson was Agnes's uncle, her mother's younger brother. He was the late son of Alexander Henderson and Jane Robb, a boy of five in his mother's cottage in 1881 and a schoolboy of fourteen in 1891, when his orphaned nieces came to the house.

By March 1901 he was twenty-five, a groom who worked with horses, and the head of the household at Lime Tree Cottage. With him were his nieces, Mary and Agnes Brown, and a boarder, James Parker. Agnes depended on him for the roof over her head. A later local history describes Andrew Henderson of Lime Tree as a poet and beekeeper. The matching name and address are a research lead; the identification with Agnes’s uncle still needs independent corroboration. His whereabouts after 1901 have not been traced.

name: Thomas McKay McKenzie
story: Thomas McKay McKenzie was the man Agnes Brown married, four years after her son was born. In 1911 he was an asylum attendant at West House, the Royal Edinburgh Asylum in Morningside, where Agnes was a nurse. His father was John Alexander McKenzie, a coastguardsman, and his mother, Mary McKay, had died.

They married by declaration at 34 Chambers Street, Edinburgh, on August 28, 1911. He was twenty-one; Agnes was twenty-five. Their daughters, Mary Christina and Jean Henderson McKenzie, were born in 1912 and 1914. On December 9, 1915, Thomas attested for the army, giving his work as barman and his family's address as 62 Balcarres Street, Morningside. He served at home from 1916 to 1919. There was no son on his family form.

name: Mary and Jean McKenzie
story: Mary Christina McKenzie and Jean Henderson McKenzie were Laurence's half-sisters, the daughters of Agnes Brown and Thomas McKay McKenzie. Mary was born at ten in the morning on May 6, 1912, at 9 Stewart Terrace, Edinburgh. Jean was born in Edinburgh in August 1914, the month the war began, and carried the surname of Agnes's mother's people.

In December 1915 their father's army papers listed them with their mother at 62 Balcarres Street, Morningside. Across the Firth of Forth, in Dunfermline, their half-brother was growing up as Laurence Douglas.

name: Alexander Archibald
story: Alexander Archibald was the gardener at Shieldhill. He was the son of a widow, Ann Archibald, born Ann Purves, and the brother of Mary and John. In April 1891, at twenty, he lived in the row of cottages called Castle at Quothquan and broke stones for the county roads. That spring Agnes, five, came to live in her grandmother's cottage a few doors along.
That June his brother John died at eighteen, twelve days after Agnes's grandmother. In December 1897 his mother died.

In 1898 Nathaniel Dunlop bought Shieldhill. By the 1901 census Alexander was a domestic gardener. The household listed at “Shieldhill” included Alexander, thirty, his wife Annie, twenty-six, born at Carnwath, and Susan Cumisky, a servant. The census does not specify their building.

The family remembers a gardener taking Laurence in. Alexander’s recorded occupation and his sister’s 1901 residence explain why he is a person of interest. No record found so far identifies him as the person who housed Agnes or took charge of her son.

name: Mary Archibald
story: Mary Archibald was a sewing mistress and the sister of Shieldhill’s gardener. She was born on October 23, 1864, at Libberton (the 1891 and 1901 censuses give her age as 27 and 35), the daughter of George Archibald and Ann Purves, and grew up in the row of cottages at Quothquan. When Agnes, five, came to her grandmother's cottage in 1891, Mary was a grown woman a few doors along, one of the first Agnes knew outside her own family.

In 1891 her brother John died, and in December 1897 her mother. At about the same time Mary had a daughter, Annie P. R., who lived until 1992. In 1901 she was a sewing mistress living alone at Gean Tree; her daughter, about three, was not with her. Her brother Alexander was the gardener at Shieldhill House.

Mary was recorded at Gean Tree Cottages in 1901. Agnes gave Gean Cottage as her own address in 1907. The gap between the records leaves open whether they shared a home. Mary later married John Cuthbertson, who is named on her gravestone at Biggar.

name: Ann Archibald
story: Ann Archibald, born Ann Purves, was the mother of Mary, Alexander and John Archibald. In April 1891 she was fifty-four, a widow and a crofter, living in the row called Castle at Quothquan, near Jane Henderson, with her three children and a visitor, Isabella Purves.

Her son John, a farm servant, died on June 20, 1891, at eighteen. Ann died on December 10, 1897, and her name is cut on the Archibald family stone at Libberton. Her children Mary and Alexander are at the heart of what happened to Agnes Brown in 1906 and 1907.

name: James Lawson Parker
story: James Parker was the boy Jane Henderson raised as her own. He was born at Biggar about 1872, and in 1881, at eight, the census found him in her cottage. In 1891 he was still there, eighteen, an agricultural laborer, when Agnes, five, came to the house. He was thirteen years older than she was, something between an uncle and an older brother.

In 1901 he was twenty-eight, a gamekeeper, boarding at Lime Tree Cottage with Andrew Henderson and his two nieces. On August 28, 1903, at Coldstream, in the parish of Carluke, he married Janet Crawford Stewart, a shepherd's daughter, and signed his full name: James Lawson Parker. He named his parents as Benjamin Parker, a mason, and Jane Lawson, a lady's maid, both dead.
He brought his wife home to Shieldhill. In 1911 he was thirty-eight, living at 3 Shieldhill Mains with Janet and three children, John, Euphemia and Robert.

name: Sir Nathaniel Dunlop
story: Nathaniel Dunlop owned the Shieldhill estate when Laurence was born. He was born at Campbeltown on April 7, 1830, served the Allan Line, the Glasgow shipping company whose steamers carried tens of thousands of Scottish emigrants to Canada, for half a century, and was chairman of the Clyde Navigation Trust.

In 1898 he bought Shieldhill from the Chancellor family, and with it the village of Quothquan and its cottages. He rebuilt houses in the village, and in 1903 he and his daughter, Ellen, put up Shieldhill Hall for evening services. He had been a widower since 1867. On June 28, 1907, his name was in the King's birthday honours, and on July 15 he was knighted at Buckingham Palace as Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill, Biggar.

In the newspapers of those years: on May 4, 1906, the Motherwell Times reported his application, as Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill, Biggar, for a water supply to the houses he owned at Quothquan. In April 1907 the Hamilton Advertiser's Biggar column noted him at a ceremony in Glasgow. On June 6, 1907, eight days before Laurence was born, The Scotsman carried an advertisement for leases on the Shieldhill Estate. On June 28, 1907, the Morning Post's list of new knights described him as residing at Shieldhill, Biggar, a justice of the peace for Lanarkshire and for Glasgow. (Sources: British Newspaper Archive.)

He was called Doctor in print. The University of Glasgow made him an honorary Doctor of Laws (LL.D.) at its graduation ceremony on Tuesday, April 23, 1907, in the presence of the Prince and Princess of Wales, as the Hamilton Advertiser's Biggar column reported on April 27. Before that, the papers called him Mr Nathaniel Dunlop. From then on, newspapers named him "Dr. Nathaniel Dunlop": the Naval & Military Record of June 6, 1907, listing guests at the King's turbine yacht; the Daily Record of June 22, 1907, quoting his speech aboard the Marmion; and the Liverpool Journal of Commerce of October 24, 1907, as chairman of the Clyde Navigation Trust. (Source: British Newspaper Archive.)
He died at Shieldhill on November 15, 1919. His will names his daughter, nephews and nieces, his household staff and charities.

name: Ellen Dunlop
story: Ellen Smith Dunlop was the only child of Sir Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill. Her mother died within weeks of her birth, and she became her father's constant companion. She never married.
In 1903 she and her father built Shieldhill Hall in Quothquan for evening worship and winter lectures. At her death in 1958 it passed to the Church of Scotland.

A shrewd manager, she financed the Thankerton Creamery in 1911, the first in Lanarkshire, partly to spare farm wives and servants the drudgery of hand dairying. She helped found the Quothquan Women's Rural Institute in 1918, bred prize Highland cattle and fed the garden birds every day.

The papers kept track of the hall. On April 13, 1912, the Hamilton Advertiser's Quothquan column reported an amateur concert held in Shieldhill Hall. On November 16, 1918, the same column reported that on Thursday, November 7, a meeting in Shieldhill Hall, Quothquan, addressed by Miss Nannie Brown of the Board of Agriculture and Miss E. B. Mitchell of Langlees, Biggar, voted unanimously to form a Women's Rural Institute in Quothquan, with 31 members. (Source: British Newspaper Archive.)
She ran Shieldhill herself after 1919 and died in 1958, aged 89, leaving much of her estate to her staff, above all her maid and companion of fifty years.

name: Shieldhill Estate and House
story: Shieldhill was the estate on the hill above the village of Quothquan, in the parish of Libberton in Upper Clydesdale, four miles from Biggar. Its house was a rambling mansion built around an old tower, with stonework of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and additions of about 1820. Below the house lay the village of Quothquan, with the row the census of 1891 called Castle, where Agnes Brown grew up.

The Chancellor family held the lands of Shieldhill from 1434, when George Chancellor was granted them with part of Quothquan. Shieldhill became the family's main home after their house at Quothquan was destroyed, following William Chancellor's support for Mary Queen of Scots at the Battle of Langside. The family buried their dead in the ruined old kirk at Quothquan, which they had taken as a family burial place around 1780. In 1898 they sold Shieldhill to Nathaniel Dunlop, a Glasgow shipowner of the Allan Line. Dunlop rebuilt Huntfield Place, turning six houses into four, enlarged the smith's house, and in 1903, with his daughter, Ellen, put up Shieldhill Hall in the village for evening services.

On census night in 1901 Alexander Archibald, his wife Annie and Susan Cumisky were enumerated at “Shieldhill.” Their precise building is unrecorded. Below the house, Mary Archibald lived at Gean Tree Cottages and fifteen-year-old Agnes Brown lived at Lime Tree Cottage.
Shieldhill is the place at the center of Laurence's beginning. When Agnes registered her son in Edinburgh in July 1907, she gave her home as Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar.

The house is still there, a category B listed building whose oldest surviving part is a sixteenth-century square keep. It became a country house hotel in 1959 and reopened in August 2020 after a long refurbishment. In 1997 Nelson Mandela stayed there during the Commonwealth summit in Edinburgh and planted an oak tree in the grounds.

name: Robert Douglas
story: Robert Douglas was the man who raised Laurence. He was born at 9 Canon Street, Edinburgh, on May 8, 1876, the son of Archibald Douglas, then a traveller for a wood merchant and later a forester, and Isabella Gray. On June 9, 1899, at twenty-three, a saw miller, he married Elizabeth Millar McDonald at 34 St Patrick Square by the forms of the Free Church of Scotland. Within two years he was a stone machineman, a skilled worker who cut and dressed stone by machine.

Their daughter, Janet Page Douglas, was born on April 29, 1900. Family information says a second daughter, Isabella Gray Douglas, died as an infant. By April 1911 the boy born Lawrence Brown was living in their home at 16 Lochrin Place as Laurence B. Douglas, their son. In 1912 the family moved to Dunfermline, and the school register named Robert as the boy's guardian.

His death register gives the cause as pulmonary tuberculosis, and records lupus since childhood. He died at Woodburn Sanatorium in Morningside, Edinburgh, on September 9, 1919, aged forty-three. Laurence was twelve.

name: Elizabeth Miller McDonald (Lizzie Douglas)
story: Elizabeth Millar McDonald, known as Lizzie, was the woman who raised Laurence, and the mother he named when he sailed for America. She was born at Liberton, on the southern edge of Edinburgh, on May 31, 1874. Her mother, Ann McDonald, was about twenty. Ann married Robert Alexander Hope on July 28, 1876, and in 1878 they sailed for New Zealand, leaving Lizzie, four, with her grandparents, John and Janet McDonald, at Gilmerton. The dates of the marriage and the sailing come from family trees compiled by other researchers.

She went into service at sixteen. On June 9, 1899, she married Robert Douglas, a saw miller, and for her own parents she gave the names of the grandparents who had raised her. Their daughter Janet was born in 1900. By 1911 she was raising the boy born Lawrence Brown as her son, Laurence B. Douglas, at 16 Lochrin Place. A woman who had been taken in took in a child.

Widowed in 1919, she worked as a school cleaner in Dunfermline. By 1929 she was using the surname Anderson, Mrs. Elizabeth Anderson of 39 Grieve Street, and both Janet and Laurence named her as their mother when they sailed for America. In September 1934, at sixty, she followed them. She sailed on the Letitia to Quebec and on October 2 entered the United States at Port Huron, Michigan, to live with Janet at 1518 Kostner Avenue in Chicago.

name: Ann McDonald Hope
story: Ann McDonald was the mother of Elizabeth (Lizzie) McDonald, the woman who raised Laurence. She was about twenty when Lizzie was born at Liberton in 1874. On July 28, 1876, she married Robert Alexander Hope, a laborer, at 33 Regent Park Square in Glasgow.

In 1878 Ann and Robert Hope sailed for New Zealand on assisted passages. Their son, John Rakaia Hope, was born at sea on September 26, 1878, and named for the emigrant ship. They settled at Cross Creek in the Wairarapa and raised four more children. Lizzie, four, stayed behind with her grandparents. Ann died at Cross Creek on January 13, 1915. These details come from family trees compiled by other researchers.

name: Robert Alexander Hope
story: Robert Alexander Hope married Ann McDonald, the mother of Lizzie Douglas, in Glasgow on July 28, 1876. He was born at Rigg, near Gretna, on July 14, 1852, the son of Gavin Hope and Elizabeth Millar.

In 1878 he and Ann emigrated to New Zealand, where their son John Rakaia Hope was born at sea. They settled at Cross Creek in the Wairarapa. Robert died at Pukekohe on December 3, 1930. Lizzie stayed behind in Scotland with her grandparents.

name: John and Janet McDonald
story: John McDonald and his wife, Janet, born Janet Page, raised their granddaughter Lizzie, the woman who would raise Laurence. In 1881 the census found them on the Main Road at Gilmerton, south of Edinburgh, in the country of coal pits and miners' rows: John, fifty-two; Janet, fifty-two; their son George; a daughter, Janet; a son, Alexander; and Elizabeth, six, entered as Grandchild.

When Lizzie married Robert Douglas in 1899, she gave their names as her parents: John McDonald, coal salesman, and Janet McDonald, born Page. She named her first daughter Janet Page Douglas, after the grandmother who had raised her.

name: Archibald Douglas and Isabella Gray
story: Archibald Douglas and Isabella Gray were the parents of Robert Douglas, the man who raised Laurence. They married in January 1863 in the parish of Newton, on the southeastern edge of Edinburgh. When Robert was born in 1876 at 9 Canon Street, Archibald was a traveller for a wood merchant; by 1899 he was a forester.
Their names appear in Robert's birth, marriage and death entries. Family information says Robert and Lizzie named an infant daughter, Isabella Gray Douglas, for Robert's mother.

name: Janet Page Douglas Crombie
story: Janet Page Douglas was the daughter of Robert and Lizzie Douglas, and the sister Laurence grew up with. She was born in Edinburgh on April 29, 1900, seven years before him. In 1911 they were in the same house at Lochrin Place, and in August 1912 the Queen Anne School in Dunfermline admitted them two days apart from the same address.

She left school at fourteen in August 1914, and in 1921 she was a clerkess with the Dunfermline Co-operative Society. On July 16, 1926, she married Thomas Crombie, and that September they crossed into the United States at Detroit and settled on South Kostner Avenue in Chicago.

In May 1929 she came home to Dunfermline, and in September she sailed back with Laurence on the Duchess of Bedford. The 1930 census found him in her household. In 1936 Janet had twin daughters, Betty and Jessie. She became an American citizen in 1948 and died in December 1979, her last home Maywood, Illinois.

name: Thomas Crombie
story: Thomas Crombie was the husband of Janet Douglas, Laurence's sister. He was a man from Kinross, thirty-two when they married in Dunfermline on July 16, 1926. That September they crossed into the United States at Detroit and settled on the West Side of Chicago.

When Laurence arrived in 1929, he named Thomas, his brother-in-law, at 1534 South Kostner Avenue, as the person he was going to. On the 1930 census Thomas was the head of the house, a furniture salesman, with Laurence entered as his brother-in-law. He became an American citizen on September 9, 1947.

name: Betty and Jessie Crombie
story: Elizabeth and Jessie Crombie were twin daughters of Janet and Thomas Crombie, born in Chicago on October 3, 1936. Elizabeth was called Betty. Their uncle Laurence was twenty-nine.
Jessie married Ronald H. Power in Cook County in September 1958. Betty died in Minneapolis on June 23, 2009, and Jessie at Poplar Grove, Illinois, on December 12, 2015.

name: Constance Eugenie Darcy Douglas
story: Constance Eugenie Darcy was Laurence's wife for twenty-one years. She was born on Saturday, October 12, 1912, at 410 Smith Street, Providence, the first child of Albert Blake Darcy, a printer, and Eugenie Emma Delaire. Her parents later divorced, and she grew up between their households. She trained as a hairdresser, and in 1937 and 1938 she worked on Westminster Street, a block from Laurence's work on Weybosset Street.

On October 9, 1939, she and Laurence were married in Birmingham, Alabama. They lived in San Francisco, where he dressed windows for Bond Stores, then in the Pittsburgh district, and after the war in Pawtucket and Providence. She trained at the Rhode Island School of Practical Nursing, and by 1961 she was a nurse at Roger Williams General Hospital.

Laurence died in 1961, when she was forty-eight. She kept nursing, worked eight years at Cranston General Hospital, and retired in 1974. In her last years she lived in East Greenwich. The family remembers her pleasant, congenial nature. She died on April 12, 1994, and was buried with Laurence at Saint Ann Cemetery, Cranston.

name: Albert Blake Darcy
story: Albert Blake Darcy was the father of Constance, Laurence's wife. He was born on November 20, 1888, at Rumford, in East Providence, the first child of John F. and Maggie Darcy, whose family had come from Ireland. By 1910, at twenty-one, he was an apprentice on a Monotype machine, learning to set type.

On January 16, 1912, he married Eugenie Emma Delaire, seventeen. Their daughter Constance was born that October, and their son Albert Norman in 1915. He moved where the work was, to Boston and Taunton and back to Providence, where he set type for the Pawtucket Times and later the Providence Journal. The marriage ended in divorce; on August 1, 1929, he took out a marriage license in Brooklyn, New York, to marry Theresa B. Sullivan, and settled at Shawomet, in Warwick.

In 1950 the census found him at 60 West Shore Road, Warwick, with Theresa, still a linotype operator in newspaper publishing. His mother, Margaret Jane Darcy, died at his house there in 1942. He died on November 4, 1957, sixteen days short of his sixty-ninth birthday, and was buried at Mount Saint Mary Cemetery in Pawtucket.

name: Eugenie Emma Delaire Darcy
story: Eugenie Emma Delaire was the mother of Constance, Laurence's wife. She was born at Sutton, Quebec, the daughter of Timothy and Julia Delaire, one of the many French Canadian families who came down to New England. She married Albert Blake Darcy in Providence on January 16, 1912, at seventeen. Her widowed mother, Julia, boarded with them on Smith Street the next year.

By 1930 she was divorced, the head of her own household at 111 Pratt Street, working as an interior decorator at a rug works. In the mid-1930s she and Constance shared a home, at Abbott Street and then Dartmouth Avenue. She died in 1966 and was buried at Saint Ann Cemetery in Cranston.

name: Albert Norman Darcy
story: Albert Norman Darcy was the younger brother of Constance, Laurence's wife. He was born at Taunton, Massachusetts, on December 7, 1915. On October 16, 1940, the same day Laurence registered for the draft in San Francisco, Albert signed his own draft card in Warwick, Rhode Island, and named his wife, Claire.
He died on October 1, 1954, aged thirty-eight, and was buried at Saint Ann Cemetery in Cranston, in section 5, lot 84. Laurence was buried in the same lot in 1961.

name: Rev. John Picken
story: The official parish minister list records John Picken as minister of Libberton and Quothquan from 1890 to 1934.

The parish history says that a Sunday service at the Quothquan religious hall, built in 1903, was conducted at 6 p.m. by Rev. John Picken, alternating with Rev. Dr. Inglis Wardrope of Moat Park Church, Biggar. The account does not date this alternating arrangement, so it cannot by itself place Wardrope at the hall in 1906–07.
No church entry naming Laurence has been identified in this review.

story: Biggar Kirk’s list gives C. Ross Lowden’s Moat Park appointment in 1900 and William Rutherford’s in 1909. Lowden is therefore the relevant Moat Park minister to investigate for 1906–07.
The minister list does not establish the family’s church membership or the arrangements for regular Shieldhill services. See the linked contemporary event reference and source comparison.

name: C. W. Inglis Wardrop
story: Biggar Kirk dates C. W. Inglis Wardrop’s Moat Park appointment to 1916. His mention in the parish’s recollection of alternating services belongs to later history and does not establish his involvement in 1906–07.
The parish account uses the spelling Wardrope. Both spellings are retained in the research guide.

name: Rev. William Whyte Smith, B.D.
story: The 1899 marriage register for Robert Douglas and Elizabeth Miller McDonald names the officiating minister as W. Whyte Smith, B.D., of Newington Free Church. The entry records the marriage on June 9, 1899, at 34 Saint Patrick Square, Edinburgh, according to the forms of the Free Church of Scotland.

A minister chronology records William Whyte Smith’s Newington appointment from 1885 and his death on March 1, 1904. The marriage entry documents his role at that ceremony; it does not establish that the Douglas family were regular members or attendees of Newington Free Church.
